case_info.scenario: A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.
case_info.caption: T1 turbo spin-echo fat-saturated magnetic resonance images of the brain through the skull base at presentation.
case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Clinician's current statement]
Given the progressive neurological symptoms and the prior history of melanoma, the most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a repeat MRI of the brain and cervical spine with contrast. This will help assess for any possible metastatic disease or other structural abnormalities that may not have been visible on the initial unenhanced MRI. The clinical presentation, especially the unilateral facial weakness and sensory changes, raises concern for a potential compressive etiology that could be related to malignancy.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

[Clinical case]
A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

[Case]

His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.

       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. case_info.caption: T1 turbo spin-echo fat-saturated magnetic resonance images of the brain through the skull base at presentation.
case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.

{
  "overall_relation": "supported" | "contradicted" | "insufficient" | "mixed" | "unknown",
  "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low",
  "reasoning": "<substantive clinical reasoning, 3-5 sentences>",

  "optional_claim_checks": ["<specific sub-claim>", ...]

For "reasoning": give the distilled MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE for this turn (3-5 sentences) — the key clinical
facts that decide this case, WHY the clinician's claim holds this relation, and specifically what the
clinician is getting right, getting wrong, or missing. This reasoning is handed to the dialogue policy as
its grounded environment knowledge, so make it clinically informative, not merely a verdict.
For "confidence": how certain you are in this relation given the available evidence.

case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

case_info.scenario: A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. case_info.caption: T1 turbo spin-echo fat-saturated magnetic resonance images of the brain through the skull base at presentation.
case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

case_info.scenario: A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. There was no afferent pupillary defect. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. His speech was slightly slurred. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. There were no other neurological abnormalities. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic. Hemoglobin A1cwas 6.8%. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.Figure 1shows the MRI at presentation.
case_info.caption: T1 turbo spin-echo fat-saturated magnetic resonance images of the brain through the skull base at presentation.
case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

case_info.explanation: C. Perineural spread of cutaneous malignancy The MRI of the brain and orbits revealed asymmetric enhancement of the right CNs V and VII, with denervation atrophy of the masticator space (Figure 2). Biopsy of the infraorbital nerve revealed squamous cell carcinoma, thought to have originated from a cutaneous source given his history. Immunotherapy was initiated with cemiplimab. MRI findings have remained stable over the past 2 years with no progression of disease or worsening symptoms. The onset of multiple cranial neuropathies presents a diagnostic dilemma. Oncological diagnosis is often difficult in the absence of an obvious lesion and normal or equivocal imaging.1This can lead to diagnostic delays and worse outcomes. This patient was seen by 20 different physicians over 5 years, including general, autonomic, and neuromuscular neurologists and neuro-ophthalmologists, before a diagnosis of malignancy was made. It can take time for perineural invasion (PNI) to become radiographically apparent, and a high index of suspicion for underlying malignancy must be maintained even with initially negative imaging. Primary leptomeningeal lymphoma (A) is a rare manifestation of primary central nervous system lymphoma that can present with multiple cranial neuropathies.2CSF results are usually abnormal and progression of symptoms more rapid.2Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (B) can present with painful ophthalmoplegia and multiple cranial neuropathies; however, steroids are typically effective.3When located along the sphenoid wing, meningiomas (D) can cause multiple progressive cranial neuropathies.4Typically visible on MRI as extra-axial homogenously enhancing masses,4no such lesion was observed here. In this patient, the symptomatology, history, and radiographic findings are best explained by PNI of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which a biopsy confirmed. One of the most common cancers in the world, cSCC occurs frequently in the head and neck secondary to sun exposure.5PNI refers to the process of tumor spread into nerves and the space surrounding them.6An estimated 2% to 6% of patients with cSCC of the head and neck will have PNI.1,6Cranial nerves V and VII are most commonly involved given their extensive anatomical distributions.1,5,6Clinically or radiographically apparent PNI confers a poor prognosis with a reported 5-year absolute survival rate of 50%.5 Treatment for cSCC of the head and neck includes surgery (if resectable) and high-dose radiotherapy and systemic therapy as appropriate. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibition is being used with increasing frequency and notable effectiveness.5-9Early-phase studies demonstrated impressive response rates near 50% for advanced, unresectable, and metastatic cSCC of the head and neck, earning US Food and Drug Administration approval for 2 checkpoint inhibitors in this setting.7,8Recently, a landmark phase 2 trial of neoadjuvant cemiplimab for stage II through IV (M0) cSCC before surgery was published, with 51% complete pathological response rates and 68% objective response rates on imaging.9Similarly, in a recent report of 11 patients with cSCC of the head and neck with clinical PNI treated with checkpoint inhibitors, radiographic disease control was observed in 9 of 11 patients at extended follow-up.5Many of these responses are durable and curative. The presence of both CN V and VII symptoms in a patient with a history of head and neck cSCC should raise suspicion for perineural recurrence of disease. While initial MRI may be negative, radiographic manifestation of PNI often occurs over time as the disease progresses and symptoms worsen. Expert review by a neuroradiologist can be helpful in identifying this finding earlier in the disease course. Mounting evidence suggests that immunotherapy is a promising treatment option for this population and should be considered as first-line therapy.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth.
